deep.reconstruction:
Context: the first line, 'stetig ist.', completes a sentence begun on the previous page: 'Die Punkte einer Geraden (t) können nicht umkehrbar eindeutig auf eine Ebene (x,y) abgebildet werden, wenn eine der beiden Functionen etwa x(t) stetig ist.' In modern terms the claim is: there is no bijection t -> (x(t), y(t)) from R onto R^2 in which one coordinate function, say x, is continuous.

(A) Composition and continuity.
(i) If f and g are continuous, then f∘g is continuous. This is standard.
(ii) A continuous function of a discontinuous function, and a discontinuous function of a continuous function, may be continuous or discontinuous.
  - Examples (mine): f constant and g arbitrary gives f∘g constant, hence continuous. If g is discontinuous at 0 only and f is continuous with range avoiding 0, e.g. f(x) = x^2 + 1, then g∘f is continuous. With f = id, the composite inherits the discontinuity.
(iii) The same holds for a discontinuous function of a discontinuous function. Hilbert's example is the inverse of a discontinuous bijection. If f is a discontinuous one-to-one function, then f^{-1}∘f = id, which is continuous.
  - The closing gloss 'Funkt. = umkehrbar eindeutige stetige Funktion' appears to mean that the composite is the identity, a one-to-one continuous function.
  - A concrete such f (mine): f(x) = x for rational x and f(x) = x + 1 for irrational x. It is a bijection of R, discontinuous everywhere, and its inverse is likewise discontinuous. This ties in with the previous page's remark on everywhere-discontinuous bijections.
  - A struck-through/hesitant aside reads 'Oder besser: unst. F von ein. st. = unst. etc.', apparently trying to tabulate the cases.

(B) No slowest convergent (divergent) series.
Claim: given a convergent (or divergent) series, one can always find one that converges (diverges) 'more slowly'. Precisely, if sum a_n converges with a_n > 0, there is a convergent sum b_n with lim b_n/a_n = ∞.
  - The word 'convergentere' is used, but the defining condition b_n/a_n -> ∞ means slower convergence.
  - The divergent analogue (implicit) is a divergent sum b_n with b_n/a_n -> 0.
Proposed 'Methode': spread each term a_k into k equal pieces a_k/k:
  a_1 + a_2/2 + a_2/2 + a_3/3 + a_3/3 + a_3/3 + ...
  - The new series c_n has the same sum, so it converges.
  - Its n-th term is c_n = a_k/k where n ≈ k^2/2, i.e. k ≈ sqrt(2n).
  - Hence c_n/a_n ≈ a_k/(k·a_{k^2/2}).
  - For a_n = n^{-p} (p > 1) this is ~ const·n^{(p-1)/2} -> ∞, and for a_n = 2^{-n} it tends to ∞ enormously. So the method works for the 'usual' series.
The next page gives the general proof instead: block-wise multiplication of the terms by increasing factors once the remainder falls below 1/2, 1/4, …. The modern version is b_n = a_n·M_k for n in the k-th block, with tails chosen so that the sum of M_k·r_{N_k} is finite. Dini's version is b_n = a_n/sqrt(r_{n-1}), where r_{n-1} = sum_{j≥n} a_j. The divergent analogue is Abel–Dini: b_n = a_n/S_n, where S_n = a_1 + … + a_n.
errors:
The 'spreading' method a_1 + a_2/2 + a_2/2 + a_3/3·3 + ... does not in general give lim b_n/a_n = ∞.
- For a_n = 1/(n log^2 n) the ratio c_n/a_n ≈ a_k/(k·a_{k^2/2}) tends to 2, not ∞.
- It also presupposes monotone a_n even to compare sensibly.
- So as a general proof it is insufficient. Hilbert indeed gives a different (remainder-based) proof on the next page.
Terminology: 'noch convergentere' is defined via b_n/a_n -> ∞, i.e. a more slowly convergent series. The word is ambiguous; a faster-converging one would be trivial (b_n = a_n/n).

The tentative tabulation 'unst. F von ein. st. = unst.' (if meant as a rule) is false. A discontinuous g composed with a continuous f can be continuous, e.g. f constant, or f's range avoiding g's discontinuities. Hilbert himself says just before that it 'kann stetig oder auch unstetig sein'.

Context claim completed on this page (line → plane bijection impossible if x(t) is continuous) is false as stated.
- Take a continuous surjection R -> R whose fibres all have cardinality of the continuum, e.g. the first coordinate of a Peano-type space-filling map R -> R^2.
- Then biject each fibre with R to define y(t).
- Only the case where both coordinates are continuous is impossible (Netto 1879).

Next-page proof as transcribed is incomplete: multiplying by 2^k once the tail is < 2^{-k} gives block contributions up to ~1 each, which may diverge. One needs, e.g., tails < 4^{-k} with factor 2^k. Possibly a transcription/compression issue.

results.what: Continuity under composition; a discontinuous function of a discontinuous function can be continuous (f^{-1}∘f = id for a discontinuous bijection f)
results.modern_name: Composition of continuous functions; counterexamples for discontinuous compositions
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore of 19th-century real analysis (Cauchy, Weierstrass, Dini textbooks)

results.what: For any convergent positive series sum a_n there is a convergent sum b_n with b_n/a_n -> ∞; dually, for divergent series a more slowly divergent one exists
results.modern_name: No slowest convergent/divergent series (Abel–Dini–du Bois-Reymond theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: N. H. Abel (1828, divergent case), U. Dini (1867), P. du Bois-Reymond (1873); later Hadamard (1894)

results.what: Heuristic construction by splitting a_k into k equal parts a_k/k to slow convergence
results.modern_name: Term-splitting / regrouping heuristic (works for power-type and geometric decay, not in general)

deep.surprise_reason: Student-level lecture/reading notes on standard 19th-century material (composition of (dis)continuous functions, du Bois-Reymond's theorem on the absence of a slowest convergent series). Nothing original; the proposed method is even insufficient in general.

checkable.asserts: For a_n = 1/(n log^2 n), the split-series ratio c_n/a_n ≈ a_k/(k a_{k^2/2}) tends to 2, not ∞, so the splitting method fails in general
For a_n = n^{-p}, the ratio is 2^{-p} k^{p-1}, which -> ∞ for p>1, so the method works for power series
The splitting a_k -> k copies of a_k/k preserves the sum, e.g. pi**2/6 for a_n=1/n**2
The expression is >= 0 for 0<a<=r. This is Dini's inequality, giving that sum a_n/sqrt(r_{n-1}) converges while (a_n/sqrt(r_{n-1}))/a_n -> ∞
The Abel–Dini dual: b_n = a_n/S_n with a_n = 1/n gives b_n/a_n -> 0, while sum 1/(n log n) still diverges
